newsitem.title: INDIA: Chinese demand seen boosting India soymeal exports.
newsitem.headline: Chinese demand seen boosting India soymeal exports.

text.p: An expected surge in soymeal demand from China and an anticipated dip in oilseeds output in other Asian countries will push up India's soymeal exports in the 1997/98 (Nov-Oct) season, trade officials said on Tuesday.

"It is projected that Chinese import demand for soymeal is expected to surge," Davish Jain, chairman of the Soybean Processors' Association of India (SOPA), the country's apex soymeal trade body, told Reuters.
"If this happens, preference would come to India due to neighbourhood and we have that capacity to supply in small shipments," Jain said.
Jain said demand from the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand and Malaysia was expected to grow due to an anticipated fall in oilseeds and grains output on account of inadequate rainfall.
India's soymeal exports in the 1996/97 season are expected to remain steady at about 2.6 million tonnes, industry officials said. "China is our star buyer this year," Jain said.
Industry officials said soymeal consumption in Asian countries was growing but India was able to cater for only 25 percent of its total export demand.
"Demand is about four times what we export," Jain said. "We feel that there will be enough marketing opportunities in the coming season."
Industry officials said the country had about 5.5 million hectares under soybean due to good early rains, but deficient showers in August were causing concern.
"Sowing has been satisfactory," Jain said. "We have achieved the targeted area coverage."
SOPA deputy chairman P.C. Mutha told Reuters the final crop size depends on rains in the next 15 days.
India harvested a soybean crop of about four million tonnes in 1996/97. Traders said they expected a crop of about 4.5 to 5.0 million tonnes in 1997/98.
"In July, we had good rains," Jain said. "Therefore the soil moisture level was adequate. August has been a relatively dry month. There is some moisture stress."
Industry officials said two good spells of rain in coming days would make up for the deficit. "But if it prolongs, it will be serious," Jain said.

Traders said soymeal for exports was currently quoted at about $263-265 per tonne FAS (free alongside ship), the same as the last two weeks, but prices would gradually fall as the output projections for the new crop became clearer.
"Prices will fall as the new crop is ahead," said a leading soymeal exporter in the central city of Indore, the hub of India's soybean industry.
Industry officials said traders were hesitant to sign forward soymeal export contracts and they were waiting for the final crop outcome before finalising deals.
"Sellers are a bit cautious," Jain said. "They are waiting and watching the harvest and weather improvement (prospects) in the coming weeks."
